references.text: Jacob bought a portion of the field at Shechem, where the well (Jacob's Well) has traditionally been located. [ref:Gen 33:19|Genesis 33:19] provides the historical background for the place where Jesus sat down.
Jacob gave Joseph a plot of land at Shechem, the area where Jacob's Well was situated. [ref:Gen 48:22|Genesis 48:22] links this territory to Jacob's inheritance.

Joseph's bones were buried in Shechem, on the plot of land that Jacob had bought—the same area where Jacob's Well was located. [ref:Josh 24:32|Joshua 24:32] confirms the historical connection to the site.
The preceding verse, [ref:John 4:5|John 4:5], identifies the place as Sychar, near the plot of land Jacob gave his son Joseph, and provides the geographical context for the well.

The prophet Isaiah says that the Lord does not grow tired or weary ([ref:Isa 40:28|Isaiah 40:28]). The fact that Jesus became tired from the journey underscores his true humanity—in contrast to God's eternal power.
[ref:Heb 4:15|Hebrews 4:15] states that we have a high priest who can sympathize with us in our weaknesses and was tested in every way. Jesus' weariness at the well demonstrates his full humanity.

The Samaritan woman asks whether Jesus is greater than Jacob, who gave them the well ([ref:John 4:12|John 4:12]). This casts light back on verse 6, where Jacob's Well is introduced as the setting for the conversation.
[ref:John 1:14|John 1:14] says that the Word became flesh and made his dwelling among us. Jesus' physical tiredness at the well is a concrete expression of this theology of incarnation.

Jesus became hungry after fasting for forty days ([ref:Matt 4:2|Matthew 4:2]). As at Jacob's Well, this shows Jesus' genuine human needs—hunger and fatigue—which testify to the reality of the incarnation.
